faqs.q: How do I know if the droppings in my Jersey City basement are from rats?
faqs.a: Rat droppings are capsule-shaped and about half an inch long — much larger than mouse droppings — and they concentrate along walls, near food storage, and beside the grease-dark rub marks rats leave on the routes they run nightly. In a Van Vorst or Paulus Hook brownstone the droppings concentrate in the garden-level kitchen and the old coal vault, and the entry is usually where a later plumbing job passed through a wall nobody resealed. A rat job here is three parts: trapping out the animals present, sealing the entries (a rat needs only a half-inch gap), and cutting the food and harborage that drew them. Any baiting, where it is used at all, follows New Jersey's pesticide rules.

faqs.q: Birds nest in my Jersey City bathroom vent every spring — what can be done?
faqs.a: Usually European starlings or house sparrows, the two species New Jersey's Game Code lets us deal with directly when they damage property. The nest comes out, the vent gets cleaned of the mites and debris nests carry, and a proper vent cover with a screen behind it ends the annual tenancy. The avenue storefronts give starlings the sign cabinets, and the apartments above them get the bathroom vents; both tenants arrive in the same spring week most years. Native birds are a different matter — a chimney swift or swallow nest means timing and deterrence work only, and we will tell you honestly which bird you have before anything is touched.

Jersey City.wildlife_intro:
Jersey City stacks every kind of housing on one peninsula: brownstones in Van Vorst Park and Paulus Hook, frame rowhouses in Bergen-Lafayette and Greenville, walk-ups around Journal Square, and the older homes of the Heights on the Palisades edge. The wildlife is as urban as the housing. Rats run the alleys, the older sewer lines, and the blocks behind every food corridor, in every neighborhood. Raccoons den in the rear extensions and chimneys of the rowhouse streets, squirrels work the Heights' trees, and starlings and sparrows nest in the vents and sign cabinets along the avenues.

Attached housing changes the math. In a rowhouse or twin, one animal in a shared attic or party-wall void is every neighbor's problem, and sealing a single unit while the adjoining roofline stays open just moves the tenant sideways. We inspect the whole run of connected rooflines where access allows, coordinate timing with neighbors when entries cross property lines, and seal the full set of openings under one plan. Older masonry party walls hide voids that let squirrels travel between houses unseen — finding those routes is most of the job in attached stock. Jersey City rowhouses share walls, voids, and often a rat run, so the plan here is written for the building line, with each owner's entries itemized separately.

faqs.q: We keep catching rats around our Hoboken home — why do they come back?
faqs.a: Because the route and the restaurant are still open. Norway rats commute along fence lines, ivy, and utility runs, and they stay where trash, pet food, or a bird feeder feeds them every single night. Hoboken rats commute through the rear courts like tenants with keys; sealing a single building while the court stays open and fed just changes which basement they sleep in, so the block's food storage is part of every job here. We map the runs, seal the building entries in metal and mortar — rats gnaw through foam and wood — and go over the sanitation changes that make the property stop paying out. Trapping alone, without those two halves, is a subscription, not a solution.

faqs.q: I hear scratching in my Hoboken attic at night — what could it be?
faqs.a: Night scratching narrows the list: bats at dusk, flying squirrels gliding in after dark, raccoons moving heavily, or rats running a wall route. Daytime noise would point to gray squirrels instead. In a Hoboken brownstone, night scratching in a ceiling usually means rats in the joist runs or a raccoon on the flat roof above, and the inspection starts on the roof, not in the apartment. Guessing wrong wastes money — the exits, timing, and sealing differ for each — so the inspection identifies the animal from droppings, entry size, and rub marks before any equipment is set.

Hoboken.wildlife_intro:
Hoboken is one square mile of brownstones, tenements, and converted factories, most of it four and five stories, all of it dense. There is little attic romance here; the wildlife work is ground-level and rear-yard. Rats are the constant, commuting between the rear yards, the restaurant blocks of Washington Street, and the basements of the older buildings. Raccoons work the same yards and the flat roofs, opossums turn up in the garden courts, and sparrows and starlings nest in the vents and cornices of the uptown and downtown brownstone rows.

Food decides where animals settle. Bird feeders spill seed that feeds rats at night, pet dishes sit out on porches, trash waits in cans a raccoon can open in seconds, and fallen fruit ferments under backyard trees. Removal without changing that menu is a short truce. We go over the property's food map with the homeowner — secured cans, feeders on baffled poles set away from the house, fruit picked up, grills cleaned — because the houses that stay quiet are the ones that stop advertising. The animal work and the housekeeping have to happen together. Hoboken results hinge on the rear-yard food map, cans, restaurant grease, and the shared court behind the buildings, and the plan names those fixes alongside the sealing.

faqs.q: Why do animals keep getting into homes in Bayonne?
faqs.a: Bayonne sits in northeastern New Jersey on the Hudson River waterfront, the most densely populated county in the state, and the habitat in between the houses — Hudson River waterfront and the Palisades — gives wildlife food and cover a short run from rooflines, decks and crawlspaces. Sealing every entry we find, not just the obvious one, is what ends the cycle here.

faqs.q: Do groundhogs do real damage in Bayonne?
faqs.a: They do in Hudson County: burrows under decks, sheds and foundation edges undermine slabs and channel water against the house, and garden feeding is heavy from spring through fall. Our crew traps groundhogs at active burrows and backfills and screens the site afterward.

Bayonne.wildlife_intro:
Bayonne gives our crew a Hudson mix shaped by Hudson River waterfront and the Palisades and the housing around it. Norway rats are the defining Hudson County call — older sewers, restaurant rows and shared-wall buildings in Jersey City, Hoboken, Union City and Bayonne let them travel block to block — with raccoons in chimneys and starlings and sparrows nesting in signs and vents along the commercial strips — and Bayonne is squarely part of that pattern, with raccoons and gray squirrels in attics, skunks and opossums under decks, and seasonal bat work in the older rooflines.

Jersey City and Hoboken mix brownstones, pre-war walk-ups and modern high-rises, Union City and North Bergen are dense brick multifamily on the Palisades, and Bayonne and Secaucus add older single-family and industrial-edge blocks. In fall and winter, squirrels and rodents push into warm attics and wall voids in Bayonne; spring brings denning raccoons and groundhog and skunk activity in yards, and summer is bat and mole season. Most Bayonne jobs start with a full roofline and foundation inspection, then removal and sealing of every entry we find, because closing only the obvious hole rarely holds.

faqs.q: Do you charge to inspect a Union City attic?
faqs.a: The inspection is the working visit: roofline, attic, and foundation get checked, entries get photographed, and you receive a written quote for the full job. Union City inspections include the flat roof and the rear shed as standard, because in this housing the entries are as likely to be at ankle or parapet level as at the eaves. That sequence — inspect first, quote in writing, then remove and seal — is how every job here runs, so there are no surprise line items after the animals are already out.

faqs.q: An opossum is living under my Union City deck — should I be worried?
faqs.a: Mostly about the mess, not disease: opossums are not on New Jersey's high-risk rabies list, and they are placid, slow animals that would rather play dead than fight. An opossum in a Union City yard has usually commuted along the fence lines from a den under a rear shed, and in lots this small the shed, not the house, is almost always the address to fix. They do shred insulation and vent ducts when they den in a crawlspace, so we take them out, clean up what they left, and screen the deck or crawlspace opening with buried hardware cloth. Check for young in the pouch season before assuming it is a solo tenant.

Union City.wildlife_intro:
Union City may be the densest small city in America: row on row of attached frame and brick homes and apartment buildings climbing the Palisades from Bergenline Avenue to the cliff-top streets. The wildlife is the wildlife of density. Rats run the shared alleys and older basements, raccoons den in the flat roofs and rear sheds, opossums work the small fenced yards, and sparrows and starlings take every open vent on the older buildings. There is almost no green buffer; the habitat is the housing itself.

Garages and sheds are the soft underbelly of a property. A garage door that stops a quarter-inch high, a shed set straight on soil, stored birdseed and grass seed in open bags — raccoons, rats, skunks, and opossums all read that as an invitation. Proofing means door sweeps and corner seals on the garage, hardware-cloth skirts on the shed, and feed and seed moved into lidded metal bins. Many house infestations turn out to start in the garage and commute through a shared attic or a breezeway, so the outbuildings get inspected with the house, every time. Union City entries cross rooflines constantly, so inspections here cover the connected run of houses wherever owners allow, and the sealing is scheduled as one job across them.

faqs.q: A groundhog is burrowing under my North Bergen foundation — how bad is that?
faqs.a: Worse than it looks. A groundhog burrow system runs many feet with several chambers, and soil removed from under a slab or footing leaves voids that crack concrete and channel water against the foundation. On the North Bergen slope a groundhog burrow in a terrace can drop soil out of a retaining wall two levels below the house, and mapping the full run is the only way to know what is actually undermined. We trap at the active entrances, then backfill and screen the site so the next groundhog inherits a closed burrow. Groundhogs are on New Jersey's rabies-vector list — one more reason not to corner one yourself.

faqs.q: There is heavy thumping in my North Bergen attic at night — is it a raccoon?
faqs.a: Heavy, deliberate thumping after dark is the classic raccoon signature; squirrels sound lighter and keep daytime hours. The cliff-side homes give raccoons a wooded approach straight to the roof, and the thumping calls cluster on the streets that back directly onto the park and the slope woods. We locate the entry — often a pushed-up soffit or a vent the animal has peeled back — check for a litter before anything moves, and get the family out together. Because raccoons sit on New Jersey's rabies-vector list, droppings and latrine areas in the attic get treated as contaminated material, not swept aside.

North Bergen.wildlife_intro:
North Bergen lives on the Palisades slope: older homes and apartments stacked on the hill streets above Tonnelle Avenue, garden apartments and newer construction on the flats, and the Meadowlands marsh at its western foot. The slope is the wildlife corridor. Raccoons, skunks, and groundhogs work down from the wooded cliff lots and North Hudson Park, rats hold the commercial corridors and the older buildings along Kennedy Boulevard, and squirrels and opossums fill in everywhere between. Houses backing onto the cliff woods get the full suburban rotation in an urban zip code.

Yard damage tells its own story. Groundhog burrows throw fans of excavated soil against foundations, skunks leave neat cone-shaped holes hunting grubs, and moles push ridges and mounds across lawns that were level in April. Treating the yard means reading which animal made which sign — the remedies differ completely — and fixing the conditions underneath: grub-heavy turf, brush piles, and woodpiles stacked against the house. Burrows at foundations get backfilled and screened once the animals are out; a hole simply filled with dirt is a hole an animal reopens in a night. North Bergen's slope lots terrace down toward the marsh, and burrows hide in every terrace wall, so the ground circuit here is as thorough as the roofline check.

faqs.q: Why do I hear running in my Weehawken ceiling every morning?
faqs.a: Daytime running, especially at dawn and mid-afternoon, points to gray squirrels — they commute. In the Heights the morning running tracks to the side of the house facing the cliff woods, where the trees stand closest and the oldest eave boards are. A squirrel entry is usually a gnawed widening at a gable vent, dormer cheek, or eave return, and the repair has to replace the chewed wood and back it with metal, or the next squirrel reopens it in days. One-way doors let the animals leave on their own schedule; then the opening is closed for good.

faqs.q: There is a dead-animal smell in my Weehawken house but I can't find anything — can you?
faqs.a: Yes — locating it is a method, not a guess. Smell intensity, fly activity, and the floor plan narrow it to a wall void, a crawlspace corner, or a stretch of ductwork, and we open the smallest section that lets us remove the carcass. In Weehawken's Heights homes the smell usually traces to a wall void on the cliff side, where an animal that entered at the eaves worked its way down and could not work its way back. The spot then gets disinfected and deodorized, and we check how the animal got in, because a carcass in a wall usually means an entry that is still open. Carcasses of rabies-vector species are handled with gloves and bagged, never bare-handed.

Weehawken.wildlife_intro:
Weehawken is a township of two levels: the older homes of the Heights on top of the Palisades, around Hamilton Park and the reservoir, and the newer waterfront development along the Hudson below the cliff. The Heights' housing is early-1900s singles, twins, and apartment buildings on quiet, treed streets, and it gets suburban wildlife: raccoons in chimneys, squirrels in eaves, skunks under porches. The waterfront adds rats along the commercial and marina edges and opossums working up from the cliff base. The cliff woods connect the two levels like a staircase.

Most entries are not holes animals made — they are building failures animals found. Fascia boards rot behind gutters, soffit panels sag at the seams, and a gray squirrel needs only a small gap and one afternoon to widen it. Repairs here mean replacing the rotted wood, not just covering it, then backing vents and eave returns with metal that teeth cannot work through. Paint-matched covers keep the fix invisible from the street. Gutters clogged with leaf litter matter too: standing water softens the very boards that are supposed to keep animals out. Weehawken's Heights homes are old enough that soffit and fascia failure is the default entry, and the metal-backed repair is specified here because the cliff winds test every loose panel.

faqs.q: What should I do about a skunk under my Secaucus porch?
faqs.a: Keep dogs inside after dusk and do not block the opening yourself — a skunk sealed in will spray, dig, or die under the porch, and all three are worse than the skunk. Secaucus porches near the creek banks are skunk dens often enough that February calls here are scheduled in street order; the same low, damp-edged lots produce them year after year until they are screened. We take skunks out with covered, low-stress handling, then trench and screen the porch perimeter with buried hardware cloth so the next one cannot move in. Skunks are a New Jersey rabies-vector species, so distance and calm are the whole technique.

faqs.q: How much should I budget for wildlife work in Secaucus?
faqs.a: Budget for three parts rather than one: getting the animals out, closing every entry they used, and cleaning what they left. The Secaucus budget conversation usually turns on the crawlspace: a simple chimney cap job and a full under-house screening job are the two ends of this town's range. Skipping the second part is the classic false economy — a cheap removal with open entries is usually a second removal by the next season, and the written quote separates the parts so you can see that plainly.

Secaucus.wildlife_intro:
Secaucus is a Meadowlands town with a split personality: a settled residential west side of postwar homes around Clarendon and the town center, and marsh, highway, and warehouse in nearly every other direction. Laurel Hill, the old Snake Hill, rises out of the marsh at the south end. The residential streets get raccoons in the chimneys, skunks and opossums under the decks, and squirrels in the eaves; the marsh edge adds rats around the outskirts and a steady traffic of animals along the creek banks. Most houses sit minutes from open marsh in at least one direction.

Crawlspaces collect problems quietly. A vent screen rusts through, a pipe penetration was never sealed, and within a season the space underneath the house holds opossums, skunks, or a raccoon latrine — along with the odor that rides the ductwork upstairs. The fix starts with a light and a full circuit underneath: every vent screened in metal, gaps around plumbing and wiring sealed, and any carcass or waste taken out. Where moisture is part of the draw, we say so plainly, because a damp crawlspace keeps attracting animals no matter how well it is screened. Secaucus ground is wet ground, and crawlspace screening here is specified for it, with a moisture note in every report, because a damp void under a house is a standing invitation.
